```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.5, fig.align = "center", dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 90)
```

Students who learn together have to regulate their joint work: they plan,
monitor progress, build consensus, discuss, manage the emotional climate and
adapt when something fails. Socially shared regulation is a sequence of such
acts, and its quality lies less in how often each act occurs than in what
follows what. Planning that leads to monitoring is a different process from
planning that leads to more planning. A comparison of high and low achieving
students therefore asks whether the two groups order their regulation
differently, not only whether they use different acts.

Lag sequential analysis gives the per-transition answer. Within each group,
it tests every ordered pair of acts against the frequency expected if the
next act did not depend on the current one (Bakeman & Quera, 2011). Between
groups, `compare_lsa()` asks whether a transition's departure from
independence differs more than a random relabelling of the students would
produce, and `bayes_compare_lsa()` estimates how large the difference in
transition probability is. This case study sets up the sequences, describes
the regulation transitions of each achievement group, locates the
transitions where the groups differ and checks those differences with a
Bayesian comparison.

```{r package}
library(lagdynamics)
```

## Data

`group_regulation_long` is a long event log of coded regulation acts in
collaborative learning, the long companion of the `group_regulation`
sequence data, taken from the tna package. Each row is one act.

- **Student:** `Actor` — 2,000 students; each student's acts form one
  sequence.
- **Achievement group:** `Achiever` — `High` or `Low`, the grouping variable
  of the comparison.
- **Collaboration group:** `Group` — 200 groups of students who work
  together.
- **Course:** `Course` — `A`, `B` or `C`.
- **Time stamp:** `Time` — date and clock time of the act; orders the acts
  within a student.
- **Act:** `Action` — one of nine regulation acts: `adapt`, `cohesion`,
  `consensus`, `coregulate`, `discuss`, `emotion`, `monitor`, `plan`,
  `synthesis`.

```{r data}
head(group_regulation_long)
with(group_regulation_long, table(Action))
with(group_regulation_long, table(Course, Achiever))
```

The 27,533 acts are dominated by `consensus` (6,797) and `plan` (6,623);
`adapt` (554) and `synthesis` (729) are the rarest. The course table carries
an important constraint for interpretation: course `A` holds only high
achievers and course `C` only low achievers, and only course `B` holds both.
Achievement and course are therefore largely confounded, and every
difference between the groups below is also, in part, a difference between
courses.

```{r nesting}
aggregate(cbind(students = Actor, achievement_levels = Achiever) ~ Group,
          data = group_regulation_long,
          FUN = \(x) length(unique(x))) |>
  summary()
```

Every collaboration group has 10 students, all with the same achievement
level. Students are nested in collaboration groups, and the 1,000 students in
each achievement group come from 100 collaboration groups.

## How are the sequences built?

In a long log, a sequence is defined by the columns that bound it. With
`actor = "Actor"`, each student's acts form a sequence, ordered by `Time`.
When a time column is given, `lsa()` also starts a new sequence whenever two
consecutive acts of a student are more than `time_threshold` seconds apart
(900 seconds, 15 minutes, by default). The largest gap between consecutive
acts of each student shows whether that rule splits anything here.

```{r gaps}
aggregate(cbind(largest_gap_s = as.numeric(Time)) ~ Actor,
          data = group_regulation_long,
          FUN = \(x) max(diff(sort(x)))) |>
  summary()
```

No student has a gap longer than 500 seconds, so the default threshold keeps
each student's acts in one sequence. A shorter threshold would cut through
the ordinary pace of the work.

```{r sessions}
lsa(group_regulation_long, actor = "Actor", action = "Action",
    time = "Time") |>
  summary() |>
  as.data.frame()
lsa(group_regulation_long, actor = "Actor", action = "Action",
    time = "Time", time_threshold = 300) |>
  summary() |>
  as.data.frame()
```

With the default threshold the log yields 2,000 sequences, one per student,
and 25,533 transitions. A 300-second threshold splits the same log into
12,305 sequences and keeps only 15,228 transitions, because every
transition across a gap is dropped. Gaps of up to
about eight minutes between the acts of a student working in a group are part of
one session, not a break between sessions, so the analysis keeps the
default.

## Which transitions characterise each group?

`group = "Achiever"` fits one model per achievement group. Both fits share
the same nine states, so their tables are directly comparable.

```{r group-fit}
g <- lsa(group_regulation_long, actor = "Actor", action = "Action",
         time = "Time", group = "Achiever")
summary(g)
```

Each group contributes 1,000 sequences; the high achievers have 12,721
transitions and the low achievers 12,812. In both groups the independence
model fails (G² = 6,147 and 7,715 on 64 degrees of freedom), and 66 and 67 of
the 81 transitions are significant. With more than 12,000 transitions per
group almost every cell is significant, so the comparison of the groups
rests on the size of the effects rather than on the significance flags. The
frequent over-represented transitions, those observed at least 400 times, are
the backbone of each group's regulation.

```{r backbone}
transitions(g, direction = "over", min_count = 400, sort = "strength")
```

Both groups share a common core. `emotion` to `cohesion` is the strongest
transition in both (z = 40.6 for high and 41.7 for low achievers, lift 4.43
and 5.32): an emotional expression is followed by an act of group cohesion.
`consensus` leads to `coregulate` and to `plan` in both groups, and `plan`
persists in both. The groups differ in what surrounds this core. Among the
high achievers, `cohesion` leads on to `consensus` (z = 19.1), `discuss`
leads to `consensus` (z = 17.0), `consensus` returns to `discuss`
(z = 14.3) and `plan` leads to `emotion` (z = 11.9); none of these reaches
400 observations with a positive residual among the low achievers. The low
achievers' backbone has one transition the high achievers' lacks, `discuss`
persisting (z = 9.5), and a stronger persistence of `plan` (1,356
transitions, z = 23.9, against 948 and z = 14.4). The high achievers'
regulation moves between discussion, consensus and cohesion; the low
achievers' stays longer within planning and within discussion.

## Where do the groups differ?

`compare_lsa()` tests the groups transition by transition. Its default
measure is the log odds ratio of each transition, a measure of the departure
from independence that does not grow with the number of transitions. The
test permutes the achievement label of whole students, R = 1,000 times, and
compares each observed difference with its permutation distribution.
Transitions with fewer than 5 pooled observations are not tested, and the
p-values are adjusted for the number of transitions tested with the
Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate procedure (`adjust = "BH"`).

```{r compare}
set.seed(2026)
cmp <- compare_lsa(g, R = 1000, adjust = "BH")
cmp
as.data.frame(cmp, what = "global")
```

The omnibus test, the sum of squared differences across all transitions,
gives p = 0.001, the smallest value 1,000 permutations can produce: the two
transition structures differ. 78 of the 81 transitions are tested and 39 of
them differ after the adjustment. The strongest differences:

```{r compare-edges}
transitions(cmp, significant = TRUE, sort = "strength") |> head(12)
```

`diff` is the log odds ratio of the high achievers minus that of the low
achievers. The largest differences involve the rare acts `synthesis` and
`adapt`, which is where low achievers avoid transitions much more strongly.
`cohesion` to `adapt` has a log odds ratio of -0.79 among high achievers and
-3.92 among low achievers (difference 3.13); `emotion` to `synthesis` and
`plan` to `synthesis` are avoided by both groups but far more by the low
achievers (differences 2.90 and 2.81). In the other direction, low achievers
move from `discuss` to `adapt` more than high achievers do (difference -1.24),
and they avoid the moves from `synthesis` to `monitor` and to `coregulate`
far less (log odds ratios -0.97 and -0.32, against -3.23 and -1.73). The picture is that high achievers reach
synthesis from more points of the process, while low achievers adapt and
monitor after discussion and synthesis.

The largest differences sit in rare transitions. The frequent transitions,
which carry most of the regulation, are better seen in a back-to-back barrel
plot of the twelve most frequent transitions.

```{r barrel, fig.height = 6}
plot(cmp, top_n = 12)
```

Each row is one transition; the high achievers' bar runs to the left and the
low achievers' to the right. Bar length is the transition probability, bar
colour the group's log odds ratio (blue above independence, red below), the
number at the end of each bar the observed count, and the central chip the
BH-adjusted p-value of the difference, starred when significant. A dark
border marks the group with the higher value when the difference is large.
Seven of the twelve frequent transitions differ. `discuss` to `consensus` and
`consensus` to `discuss` have long blue bars on the high achievers' side and
short, near-white bars on the low achievers' side: discussion and consensus
alternate among high achievers and not among low achievers. On the low
achievers' side, `plan` to `plan`, `discuss` to `discuss` and `discuss` to
`synthesis` are the longer bars. `emotion` to `cohesion`, the strongest
transition in both groups, does not differ.

## A Bayesian check

The permutation test compares log odds ratios. `bayes_compare_lsa()`
compares the transition probabilities themselves. It places a Dirichlet
posterior on each row of each group's table, draws from the posterior of the
difference in each transition probability and reports its 95% credible
interval. A transition is flagged as credibly different when the interval
excludes zero, the difference exceeds 0.01 and the interval bound nearest zero
exceeds 0.001. The `p_adj` column holds the
Bayesian two-sided p-values, also Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted
(`adjust = "BH"`); the flag itself is set by the credible interval.

```{r bayes}
bc <- bayes_compare_lsa(g, adjust = "BH", seed = 2026)
as.data.frame(bc, what = "global")
transitions(bc, significant = TRUE, sort = "strength") |> head(10)
```

38 of the 81 transition probabilities differ credibly. The largest
difference is `discuss` to `consensus`: 42.4% of the high achievers'
discussion acts are followed by consensus, against 21.4% of the low
achievers', a difference of 0.210 with a 95% credible interval of 0.181 to
0.238. High achievers also move from `synthesis` to `consensus` more often
(difference 0.186) and from `synthesis` to `plan` (0.118), while low
achievers move from `synthesis` to `adapt` (difference -0.16) and from
`discuss` to `adapt` (-0.096) more often.

The two comparisons answer different questions and agree where they
overlap. `discuss` to `adapt` and `synthesis` to `plan` differ on both
scales, in the same direction. `discuss` to `consensus` has the largest
probability difference and a significant log odds ratio difference that is
not among the twelve largest, because the log odds ratio discounts the high
base rate of `consensus`. Transitions among rare acts, such as `cohesion` to
`adapt`, have the largest log odds ratio differences but probability
differences too small to be flagged by the Bayesian comparison. Both tests treat each student as independent, and the next
section returns to that assumption.

## What the analysis shows

- The log yields one sequence per student; no student pauses for more than
  500 seconds, so the 15-minute session threshold splits nothing.
- High and low achievers share a regulation core: `emotion` to `cohesion`,
  `consensus` to `coregulate` and to `plan`, and persistent planning.
- The transition structures differ (omnibus permutation p = 0.001), with 39
  of 78 tested transitions differing after Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment and
  38 of 81 transition probabilities differing credibly.
- High achievers alternate between discussion and consensus and move from
  synthesis to consensus and planning; low achievers move from discussion
  and synthesis to adaptation and stay longer in planning and discussion.
- The largest differences in log odds ratio involve the rare acts
  `synthesis` and `adapt`; the largest differences in probability involve
  the frequent move from `discuss` to `consensus`.

The design limits what these differences mean. Achievement is confounded
with course: courses `A` and `C` each hold a single achievement level, so a
course effect cannot be separated from an achievement effect in these data.
A comparison restricted to course `B` would separate them. Students are also
nested in collaboration groups of 10 that share their interaction, while
both comparisons treat the 2,000 students as independent units. Within-group
dependence makes the p-values and credible intervals narrower than they
should be, so the differences near the significance threshold deserve less
weight than the large ones. Finally, the models are first order and pool all
acts of a student: they describe what follows what, not how the process
changes over a session. For the comparison methods themselves, see
[the group comparison article](group-comparison.html); for building
sequences from logs, see [the event logs guide](event-logs.html).

## References

Bakeman, R., & Quera, V. (2011). *Sequential analysis and observational
methods for the behavioral sciences*. Cambridge University Press.
